p: Where English has "the LORD" in capitals, the Hebrew has God's own name, four letters, YHWH.
b: Capital letters, "the LORD", stand for the name YHWH, which Israel stopped saying aloud and which most English Bibles follow Jewish practice in replacing with "the Lord". When the Hebrew has the title Adonay instead, the Plain writes "the Lord" in lower case. Joel uses the name on almost every page. It is the name God gave Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14-15), and the book's central promise rests on it: "you will know that I am the LORD your God" (2:27; 3:17). The Hebrew word for "word" here, davar, opens the book the way it opens Hosea, Micah and Zephaniah: a word that "came" like an event.

p: Joel means "the LORD is God". Nothing else is known of him; his father's name appears in no other book.
b: Yo'el is "YHWH is God", a common name: a dozen other men called Joel are named in the Bible (for example Samuel's older son, 1 Samuel 8:2, and a chief of Reuben, 1 Chronicles 5:4). The book says nothing about this Joel's home, tribe or work, beyond his knowledge of the Temple and the priests, whom he addresses as a group. His father's name Petu'el is not found elsewhere; the Greek Bible has Bathouel (Bethuel). The Lives of the Prophets, an early Jewish-Christian collection whose date and text are debated, says Joel came from the tribe of Reuben. That is a legend of a later age, not evidence. The Plain gives the Hebrew spelling.

a: word came to Joel, son of Pethuel
p: The book names no king and no date. Scholars put it anywhere from the 800s to the 300s BC, and most now favor the Persian period.
b: Late date (about 500 to 350 BC) is the view of most critical commentators (Wolff, Crenshaw, Barton). The Temple and priests lead the nation and no king is named; the elders and the walls of Jerusalem appear (2:7-9); the exile and the scattering of Judah are in the past (3:2); Greeks buy slaves (3:6); and the book leans on older prophets (compare Obadiah 15, 17; Isaiah 13:6; Ezekiel 30:2-3; Amos 1:2). Early date (about 830 to 800 BC) is held by some evangelical commentators (for example Stuart). They note that the Hebrew Bible puts Joel between Hosea and Amos, that the enemies named, Tyre, Sidon, Philistia, Egypt and Edom, fit the ninth century (2 Kings 8:20-22; 2 Chronicles 21:16-17), and that a boy-king's reign, with a priest in charge (2 Kings 11-12), explains why no king is named. Jewish tradition took another course: Seder Olam Rabbah places Joel in the days of Manasseh, a late date before the exile; this edition found no Jewish authority for a ninth-century date. The text itself does not settle the question, and the Plain does not.

a: Has this ever happened in your days
p: The elders are asked whether anyone remembers anything like it. The answer expected is no.
b: The question is the speaker's way of saying that this plague is the worst in living memory and in the memory the elders inherited from their fathers. The same claim is made of the locusts of Egypt (Exodus 10:6, 14) and again of the army in Joel 2:2. Such language is the ordinary speech of a prophet who wants a hearing; it is not a measurement. Notice who is asked to listen: the elders and "everyone who lives in the land", not the king. The elders were the heads of families and towns and the keepers of memory, and in Joel they are called again to the assembly (1:14; 2:16).

t: A story for the next generations
p: The plague is to be told like the plagues of Egypt, so that later generations know what the LORD did.
b: Israel was told to hand down the great acts of God to children and grandchildren: the plagues of Egypt, including the locusts (Exodus 10:2), the commands of the law (Deuteronomy 6:7), and the deeds of the LORD (Psalm 78:4-6). Joel uses that old pattern for a disaster. The effect is to place this plague beside the Exodus signs and to make it part of what Israel must remember. The Hebrew has no verb in the second and third lines; they carry on the command of the first, so the sense is "let your children tell their children, and let those children tell the next generation", and the Plain follows that. The chain has four links: you, your children, their children and the next generation, as the four locusts in the next verse come one after another.

a: The cutting locust left some behind
p: The Hebrew has four words for locust here. The Plain keeps four English words, with the cut, swarm, hop and strip of each.
b: The four words are gazam ("the cutting locust", from a root meaning to cut off), 'arbeh ("the swarming locust", the common word for locusts in Exodus 10 and from a root for multiplying), yeleq ("the hopping locust", with a root for licking or leaping; Nahum 3:15-16; Jeremiah 51:27) and chasil ("the stripping locust", from a root for consuming; Deuteronomy 28:38; 1 Kings 8:37). English versions mix "locust", "grasshopper", "caterpillar", "cankerworm" and "palmerworm", and no one is sure which insect each Hebrew word named. The Plain gives four distinct English words so that the reader can see the four steps and the four names, and uses them again in 2:25. The Septuagint gives four Greek names (kampe, akris, brouchos, erysibe; Greek 'mildew' for the last).
orig: גָּזָם, אַרְבֶּה, יֶלֶק, חָסִיל (gazam, 'arbeh, yeleq, chasil)

a: The hopping locust left some behind
t: Stages, kinds or names? And what do the four stand for?
p: Four views: four stages of one insect, four kinds of locust, four poetic names, or four invading nations.
b: Four stages. The locust grows in stages from a wingless hopper to a winged adult, and the four words may be the four stages (a view found in older commentaries). Four kinds. The four may be kinds of locust or grasshopper that swept the land in succession. Four poetic names, used for variety and for the number four, which stands for completeness: the stress is on a plague that left nothing. Modern commentators such as Wolff and Crenshaw doubt that the text lets us tell the four apart. Four nations. Jewish and Christian interpreters from late antiquity read the four as four empires that struck Israel and Judah in turn; Jerome's commentary on Joel is the usual place to see this reading and the Jewish readings it reports. Whatever the four are, the verse describes eating after eating, so that what one left the next took. The text does not say how many years the plague lasted; the later "years" of 2:25 suggests more than one season.

t: What did Rashi, Radak and Ibn Ezra say about the four?
p: Rashi calls all four species of locust; Radak says they came in turn over four years; Ibn Ezra gives roots for three.
b: Rashi, at 1:4, says that the four words are species of locust. Radak (David Kimhi) explains each name from its root (gazam from shearing, 'arbeh as the most numerous kind, yeleq from licking up, chasil from cutting everything off) and says the four came one after another over four years, so that what one left in a year the next ate in the following year. Ibn Ezra's short comment on the verse gives roots for three of the names (for example gazam as shearing) and does not take up 'arbeh. The Targum, Ephrem, Cyril of Alexandria and Theodoret on this verse were not checked for this edition.

p: The Hebrew word 'asis is fresh grape juice or sweet new wine, the first thing a drinker loses.
b: 'Asis is sweet wine, perhaps freshly pressed juice or a young wine; the same word is used again for the mountains that "drip" it in the restored land (3:18; compare Amos 9:13). Joel opens his list of losses with those who drink most and need the harvest least, the heavy drinkers. The prophets often speak harshly of drunkenness (Isaiah 5:11-12; 28:1), but here the point is not a sermon on drink. It is a simple, vivid sign: when the vines fail, even the drunk wake up, because there is nothing left to drink. The loss of wine is also the loss of what went into the drink offering in the Temple (1:9).

a: A nation has marched onto my land
p: The locusts are called a nation with lion's teeth. Is this a swarm told as an army, or an army told as a swarm?
b: Proverbs 30:25-26 calls the ants and the rock badgers each "a people", and 30:27 says the locusts have no king, yet go out "in rows". Calling the insects a nation (goy) with my land is a way of saying that they behave like an invading army, and the teeth of a lion and the fangs of a lioness are the image for their jaws (Revelation 9:8 repeats it). Three readings: (1) a real locust plague, told as war; (2) a real army, whose attack is drawn with locust images (this is how some ancient and medieval readers took the book's second half); (3) a plague that the poet uses as a sign of the final day. The speaker of "my land" may be the prophet for his people, or the LORD, whose land it is (2:18; 3:2). The Hebrew does not mark the change of voice.

t: The vine and the fig tree
p: Vine and fig are the signs of a settled, peaceful life, and often of Israel itself.
b: In Israel's world the vine and the fig tree stood for safe, settled farming (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4). The prophets use the vine as a picture of Israel (Isaiah 5:1-7; Psalm 80:8-16; Hosea 10:1), and Joel's "my vine" and "my fig tree" may carry that echo, since the LORD speaks of "my land" in the verse before. Wrecking vine and fig is wrecking the nation's hope. The word for the fig tree's state, qetsafah, is rare and uncertain: "a stump", "splinters" or "foam" have all been proposed. The Plain says "a stump".

a: Wail like a young woman dressed in sackcloth
p: The command is to a single woman, and the Hebrew does not say who she is.
b: The verb "wail" is feminine and singular, unlike the plural commands around it. The most common view is that the addressee is Zion or the land personified, who is told to mourn like a young woman who has lost her husband. ("Husband" is ba'al, a word that can also mean a betrothed man, as in Deuteronomy 22:23-24, so the Hebrew does not say whether the wedding had taken place.) Another view makes her a single mourner in the crowd. "Young woman" is betulah, the normal word for a girl of marriageable age (compare Lamentations 1:15); the Plain does not say "virgin" because the verse is about her grief, not her history. "Husband of her youth" is the husband she married as a girl (Proverbs 2:17; Malachi 2:14), and the picture is of the sharpest kind of loss.

p: The morning and evening offerings of grain and wine stop. For priests this is the sign that the worst has come.
b: Each morning and evening the Temple offered a lamb with flour and a drink offering of wine (Exodus 29:38-41; Numbers 28:3-8). When the harvest fails there is no flour, no wine and no oil for these gifts, and the priests have nothing to offer. For Joel this is a double loss: the people lose the harvest, and the LORD loses his worship. The Mishnah counts the end of the daily offering among the disasters of the 17th of Tammuz, when Jerusalem was besieged (Mishnah Taanit 4:6). That Joel can say the offerings are "cut off" and "kept back" (1:13) shows that the Temple is standing and its service is in order, which matters for the date.

p: In the Bible a land can mourn: the soil itself goes into mourning when the people sin or the harvest fails.
b: The verb 'avel ("mourn") is used of people, but also of the land in Jeremiah 12:4 and 23:10, Hosea 4:3 and Isaiah 24:4. The Hebrew for "ground" here is 'adamah, the red soil that gave humankind its name (Genesis 2:7; 3:17-19). Some scholars call this the language of covenant: the earth shares the people's fate (Deuteronomy 28:38-42; Leviticus 26:19-20). Others note that the poetry is simply personifying fields that go brown. The Hebrew also repeats shuddad ("wrecked") for field and for grain.

t: Dry or ashamed? A Hebrew pun
p: Two Hebrew verbs look the same in this form: "be ashamed" and "dry up". Joel plays on both.
b: Two different Hebrew roots give the same form in the causative. The causative of bosh, "be ashamed", and the causative of yavesh, "be dry", are both hovish. The command hovishu in 1:11 is taken as "be ashamed" (or "show shame"); hovish in 1:10 (the new wine), in 1:12 (joy) and in 1:17 (the grain) is most naturally "has gone dry", and hovishah in 1:12 (the vine) can be either. The simple verb yavesh, "be dry", appears in 1:12 (every tree is dry) and 1:20 (the channels of water are dry). The pun between shame and dryness is probably on purpose: crops "dry up" and farmers "are ashamed". The same root for shame returns at the book's turn, where the LORD says "my people will never be ashamed" (2:26-27). The Plain writes "has gone dry" at 1:10 and 1:17, "Be ashamed" at 1:11, "Dry is the vine" and "is dry" in 1:12, and "joy has dried up"; English cannot carry both senses at once, and the notes show the pun.

p: Hebrew tappuach is a fruit tree of Israel. It may be the apple, the apricot or the quince.
b: Tappuach is named in the Song of Songs (2:3, 5; 7:8; 8:5) and in Proverbs 25:11. The apple was not widely grown in ancient Israel, and scholars have proposed the apricot (once believed to have been introduced late), the quince or the citron. The place name Beth-tappuah and the apple-scented breath of the Song both point to an aromatic fruit. The Plain keeps the traditional "apple", and the reader should not picture a modern orchard apple. The pomegranate, the palm (the date palm) and the apple are the fruit trees Joel names after the vine and the fig. The scroll 4Q78 (4QXII-c) lists the trees in a different order: its visible words run "the fig tree, also palm and apple" and then "pomegranate", with the word for "withered" restored between them, so the pomegranate comes after the apple. The scroll 4Q82 (4QXII-g) keeps the Masoretic order in the words that survive ("withered" follows the fig tree; "pomegranate" is restored after it), and the Greek has the Masoretic order. The trees named are the same. See the variant.

p: When the harvest fails, joy fails, and with it the festivals that were celebrated at harvest.
b: In the Bible joy and harvest go together: Israel's three great festivals were harvest festivals (Deuteronomy 16:13-15 commands joy at the Feast of Booths). When the crop fails, joy goes out of the earth, as in Isaiah 16:10 and Isaiah 24:11. For Joel this loss is also a loss of worship, since "joy and gladness" belong to the house of God (1:16). The reversal comes in 2:21-23, where the land, the animals and the people are told to rejoice again.

p: Sackcloth was a rough cloth, usually of goat hair, worn by mourners and by people pleading with God.
b: Wearing sackcloth was a public sign of grief or humbling: Jacob for Joseph (Genesis 37:34), Hezekiah before Isaiah's message (2 Kings 19:1), the Ninevites in Jonah 3:5-8. Priests are told to wear it and to spend the night in it, perhaps in the Temple precincts, in vigil. A prayer vigil with priests lying in sackcloth on the Temple floor is the setting a first hearer would picture. The order to the priests comes first because they alone can lead the nation's prayer and must also feel the loss of the offerings.

a: kept back from the house of your God
p: The priests still serve in a standing Temple; the offerings stop only because there is nothing to offer.
b: The offerings are "kept back" (nimna'), not destroyed, and the "house of the LORD" is the center of the nation's response (1:9, 14, 16; 2:17; 3:18). A date after the Babylonian destruction of the Temple (586 BC) requires a date after its rebuilding (515 BC); a date before 586 BC places the book in the First Temple. Neither is certain, and the book has no word on the building itself, which is why scholars can argue for both.

t: A fast as a holy act
p: A public fast was called by a leader and kept as a holy day. This is the first of Joel's three calls to fast.
b: To "consecrate" (qaddesh) a fast is to set apart a day for it, as a holy day. The Bible knows public fasts in a crisis (Judges 20:26; 1 Samuel 7:6; 2 Chronicles 20:3; Jeremiah 36:9; Ezra 8:21; Esther 4:16; Jonah 3:5), led by the king or by the elders and ending in a gathering at the Temple. The "sacred assembly" ('atsarah) is the same kind of gathering; the Plain also uses "sacred assembly" for this word in Isaiah 1:13, where the prophet says God cannot stand wrongdoing joined to it. Joel calls the fast three times in the book: 1:14, 2:12 and 2:15. The Mishnah (Taanit 1-3) sets out how the later community kept fasts for drought.
r: Judges 20:26; 1 Samuel 7:6; 2 Chronicles 20:3; Jeremiah 36:9; Jonah 3:5; Joel 2:12; Joel 2:15

a: the day of the LORD is close
t: The day of the LORD begins here
p: "The day of the LORD" is Joel's key phrase. It is a day when God acts, and the first reading is a plague.
b: In Joel the phrase yom YHWH occurs five times (1:15; 2:1, 11, 31; 3:14). The same words are in Isaiah 13:6, 9; Ezekiel 30:2-3; Obadiah 15; Zephaniah 1:7, 14, 18 (with near forms at 2:2-3) and Amos 5:18-20, where the day is also a day of darkness, not of light. The Plain writes "close" in 1:15 because the line is word for word Isaiah 13:6 and the Isaiah Plain has "close"; the same Hebrew word, qarov, is "near" in 2:1 and 3:14, as in Ezekiel 30:3 and Obadiah 15. Here the day is near, and what has already come, the locusts and the drought, is its first sign. The book will go on to widen the day: an army (2:1-11), a day for repentance (2:12-14), and at last the day of judgment on the nations (3:14) and of the Spirit and cosmic signs (2:28-32). See the topic page for the day of the LORD.

p: The Hebrew puns on two sounds: shod, "havoc", and Shaddai, "the Almighty".
b: Kesod mishshadday yavo sounds like "as shod from Shaddai it comes". The line is word for word the line in Isaiah 13:6, and the Plain matches the Plain of Isaiah. Which prophet borrowed from which is uncertain; scholars are divided, and the line may also come from a shared saying. Shaddai is an old name of God, in the Plain "the Almighty", whose original sense (mountain? breast? the destroyer?) is lost. Joel lets the pun carry the sense that the havoc comes from God.

p: Three rare words make this verse hard: the seeds' state, what they lie under and the granaries.
b: Each of the first three phrases has a word that appears nowhere else or is unclear: 'avshu ("shrivel", perhaps "rot"), perudot ("seeds", a rare word), megrefot ("clods", from a root for a shovel or scraper) and mammegurot ("granaries"). The Greek reads parot, "heifers", for the seeds and phatnais, "mangers", for the clods, and Jerome's Latin Bible has the animals rotting in their dung. The Plain follows the Hebrew with the most widely held sense: seeds sown in dry ground, not sprouting. See the variant. A Qumran scroll of the Twelve, 4Q78, reads the first two words differently from the Masoretic Text: its first word is spelled with a p where the Masoretic Text has a b ('afshu for 'avshu), and its second is purot where the Masoretic Text has perudot, with no d. The rest of the verse in the scroll matches the Masoretic Text. A spelling without the d can be read parot, "heifers", which is what the Greek has, or as perudot spelled with a letter lost, so the scroll is the best Hebrew support in the book for the Greek reading but does not settle the matter.

p: The Hebrew word nashamu comes from asham, "guilt" or "penalty". The animals share the blame.
b: The verb is related to asham, "guilt" or "guilt offering", and can mean "bear the guilt" or "suffer the penalty" (Hosea 5:15; 10:2; 13:16). Some commentators think it here means only "suffer" or "are desolate", a related sense. The Plain says "pay the price" and keeps both senses open. What is striking is that animals suffer in Joel and are called to the LORD as well: 1:20 and 2:22 (the animals gasp for the LORD, then are told not to fear). Jonah 3:7-8 has the animals fast and put on sackcloth.

a: I call out to you, LORD
p: The prophet turns from speaking to the people to speaking for them, in the voice of a psalm of complaint.
b: After the calls to the elders, drunkards, farmers and priests, a single voice cries out to the LORD: "I call out to you." The speaker is most likely Joel, who prays for the people and shows them how to pray (as Moses and Jeremiah do; compare Jeremiah 14:1-9). The next verse lets even the animals of the field join. The style resembles the communal laments (Psalm 74; 79; 80; Lamentations): the picture of ruin, then the cry to the LORD. This turn from the prophet's "you" to a prayer is the first half of the book's shape: what the prophet asks the people to do, he does first.

a: fire has eaten the grasslands of the wilderness
p: Is the fire a wildfire, the heat of the drought, or the picture of an invading army?
b: In 1:19-20 fire and flame burn the wilderness pastures and the trees, and in 2:3 a fire eats before the invader. Three readings: (1) literal brush fire in a drought, as in a dry summer; (2) the scorching heat that follows the locusts, whose bare ground bakes (Amos 7:4 pictures a fire that dried up the deep); (3) a picture of war, since armies burn the lands they cross (Isaiah 9:18-19). The text does not choose. It does show the LORD's own judgment at work behind the natural facts, a theme that returns when "fire" goes before the army (2:3).

p: The Hebrew verb arog is the verb of Psalm 42:1: the thirsty deer that longs for water.
b: Ta'arog ("gasp for", "long for") is used of a deer that craves streams of water in Psalm 42:1, and Joel borrows the image for all the animals of the field. The animals do not speak, but their need is a kind of prayer, and the LORD, who feeds them (Psalm 104:21, 27-28; 147:9), will answer them in 2:22. In Joel, then, the whole creation cries out, and it is the LORD's answer to the animals that comes first in the promise (2:22).

a: Blow the ram's horn in Zion
p: The shofar, a ram's horn, was the alarm of war and the call to gather. Here it summons Zion to sound the alarm.
b: The shofar was blown to warn of an enemy (Jeremiah 4:5; Hosea 5:8; Amos 3:6), to gather the community (Exodus 19:16; Judges 3:27) and at feasts and fasts. Joel blows it twice: here for alarm and in 2:15 for the fast and assembly, so the same horn that warns also calls the nation to turn back. "Sound the alarm" is hari'u, to shout the war cry or the teruah blast. The hearers are on Zion, the "holy mountain" where the LORD lives (3:17, 21).

a: the day of the LORD is coming
t: Where does "the day of the LORD" come from?
p: Scholars explain the phrase as a holy-war tradition, a festival, or a day of appearing. Joel uses it all three ways.
b: Holy war. Gerhard von Rad argued that the day was the day of the LORD's victory over Israel's enemies, drawn from the old wars of Israel (Judges 5; Isaiah 9:4). Festival. Sigmund Mowinckel connected it to an autumn festival of the LORD's kingship. Appearance. Meir Weiss traced it to the tradition of the LORD appearing in storm, light and shaking (Judges 5:4-5; Psalm 18; Habakkuk 3). Amos turned the hope on its head: for sinful Israel it is "darkness, not light" (Amos 5:18-20). Joel uses the day as a day of disaster (1:15; 2:1-11), as a day of turning (2:12-17), as a day of cosmic signs and rescue (2:30-32) and as a day of judgment on the nations (3:14-16). See the topic page.
r: Amos 5:18; Isaiah 13:6; Zephaniah 1:14; Obadiah 15; Joel 1:15; Joel 3:14

a: Like dawn spread over the mountains
p: The same letters can be read "dawn" or, as some scholars read them, a rare word for "blackness"; every ancient witness has "dawn".
b: The Hebrew has shachar, "dawn", and the Greek has "dawn" too. The verse before has the day of darkness and cloud; the line then pictures a mass coming over the mountains like dawn, perhaps the way the first light spreads over the hills, quickly and from the edge of the sky; or a vast army that appears at dawn. Some read shachor, "blackness", a darkness that spreads, because a swarm of locusts can darken the sky (compare Exodus 10:15). The scroll 4Q82 (4QXII-g) preserves the words "like dawn spread" with the same consonants; no manuscript marks the vowels differently, so the choice between the readings rests on the context. The Plain keeps "dawn", the text that all ancient witnesses have. See the variant. The Plain also keeps the Hebrew order of the first line, "darkness and gloom".

a: Nothing like it has happened since long ago
p: The same claim was made of the locusts of Egypt. In Joel it covers the whole generation.
b: Exodus 10:6 and 10:14 say of the Egyptian locusts that nothing like them had been seen and none like them would be seen again. Joel borrows the words for the army that follows the plague of chapter 1 (compare 1:2). Such sweeping claims are common in the Bible for great judgments (Exodus 11:6; Daniel 12:1; Matthew 24:21) and are not the result of a careful survey; they say how the speaker feels. The Plain follows the Hebrew: "through the years of all generations" (literally "to the years of generation and generation").

t: Eden before and a desert behind
p: Joel uses Eden as the picture of a fertile land, and then turns it upside down.
b: Isaiah 51:3 and Ezekiel 36:35 promise that the desolate land will become "like Eden" and "like the garden of Eden". Joel does the opposite: the land is a garden when the army reaches it and a wilderness when the army has passed. The phrase "the garden of Eden" (gan 'eden) is used in Ezekiel 28:13 and 31:9, and Genesis 13:10 compares the plain of the Jordan to "the garden of the LORD", Lot's choice. Joel 2:3 is one of the few places where Eden is a picture of what is about to be destroyed; Ezekiel 31:9 and 31:16-18 use the trees of Eden for the fall of a great tree. In the end the LORD makes a spring flow "from the house of the LORD" (3:18), and the picture is reversed again.

p: Many languages have noticed that a locust's head looks like a small horse. So do the Greek and Hebrew of the Bible.
b: The face of a locust, long and blunt, is said to look like a horse's. Italian calls the grasshopper cavalletta, "little horse", and German calls it Heupferd, "hay-horse". Job 39:20 compares a horse's leap to that of the locust ('arbeh). Revelation 9:7 describes locusts as "like horses made ready for war", which is probably a use of Joel. A swarm in motion also makes a loud whirring (Revelation 9:9 and Joel 2:5 compare it to chariots). Whether Joel is describing insects or an army that looks like insects is debated at 1:6; this verse works equally well for both.

t: A word used in Nahum too
p: The Hebrew paror is a rare word. Some read "lose color", others "glow" or "blackened like a pot".
b: The Hebrew says that faces "gather paror", and the same phrase is in Nahum 2:10. The sense is disputed: "gather a glow" (flush with fear), "withdraw their color" (go pale), or "gather blackness" (as the soot on a cooking pot, parur, Numbers 11:8). The Greek translator read "as the scorching of a pot". The Plain takes "loses its color", the most common modern view. The words are an image of fear, the face draining of blood or darkening; the sense is the same.

a: Each one marches on his own road
p: The description of an orderly army fits the way a locust swarm moves, without leaders and without turning.
b: Proverbs 30:27 says of the locusts that they "have no king, but out they go in rows, every one of them". Joel 2:7-8 draws on the same observation: they march each on his own track, do not push each other, and do not leave the path. The effect is of discipline, as in a trained army. Observers of swarms report just this: the hoppers move in bands in one direction, climbing over walls, trees and houses. See the note on 1:6 about whether Joel means locusts or an army, or both at once.

p: The word shelach may mean a missile, a javelin or a sword. Or it may mean a water channel.
b: Shelach appears in Job 33:18; 36:12 ("to die by the shelach") and 2 Chronicles 23:10 for a missile or weapon, and Nehemiah 3:15 names "the Pool of Shelah", so its sense is not fixed. Most take it as weapons, which fits the swarm that cannot be stopped by throwing or striking. The next word, yivtsa'u, is also unclear ("break ranks", "be cut down", "be harmed"). The Plain says they "do not stop", the sense of the whole line.

p: Joel's "thief" at the windows is the first of several passages that say the day will come like a thief.
b: The New Testament says that the day of the Lord comes "like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10; compare Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39; Revelation 3:3; 16:15). The wording there is not a direct quotation of Joel, whose thief climbs in at the windows during a raid, but the image of the day coming unseen and unwelcome fits the way Joel presents the day of the LORD in this chapter. See the topic page on the day of the LORD.

a: The sun and moon grow dark
t: Signs in sun, moon and stars
p: The prophets describe the day of the LORD with darkened sun, moon and stars. Joel uses the picture three times.
b: Joel 2:10, 2:31 and 3:15 all picture the sun, moon and stars failing. The same images are in Isaiah 13:10 (the day of the LORD against Babylon), Ezekiel 32:7-8 (Egypt), Amos 8:9, Matthew 24:29, with Mark 13:24-25 and Luke 21:25-26 (the Plain of Matthew: "the sun will turn dark, the moon will not shed its glow, the stars will fall from the sky"), Acts 2:20 and Revelation 6:12 ("the sun became black like sackcloth made of hair, and all of the moon became like blood"). Readers have taken them as the real sky, as the picture of an overthrown empire, or as poetry for the end of an age. The darkness may also recall the plague of darkness in Egypt (Exodus 10:21-23) and the swarm that darkens the sky (Exodus 10:15). See the topic page on signs in the sky.
r: Isaiah 13:10; Ezekiel 32:7; Amos 8:9; Matthew 24:29; Acts 2:20; Revelation 6:12; Mark 13:24; Luke 21:25

a: at the head of his army
p: The army that has been terrifying the land turns out to be the LORD's own.
b: In 1:6 the "nation" came up against "my land"; here the army is "his army" and the camp is "his camp". In 2:25 the locusts are "my great army that I sent among you". Joel therefore says that the plague and the army are the LORD's instruments, as the Assyrians are in Isaiah 10:5-6 and the Babylonians in Habakkuk 1:6. This is why the same LORD can be asked to turn back and relent: the destroyer is under his command (2:12-14). The Plain keeps the Hebrew "army" and "camp".

p: The question has no answer in the verse. Other prophets ask it too.
b: "Who can endure the day of his coming?" asks Malachi 3:2; Nahum 1:6 asks who can stand before the LORD's anger; Revelation 6:17 asks who can stand. In Joel the question is an invitation: the next verse turns "Who can bear it?" into "Even now, turn back". The only answer the book gives is that those who turn to the gracious God will be spared (2:12-14, 32). The scroll 4Q78 (4QXII-c) reads a different form of the verb here, "sustain it" for "bear it", with the same sense, and spells the word for "very" with an extra letter; in 4Q82 (4QXII-g) the verb is restored, so it gives no second witness.

p: The Hebrew ne'um YHWH means "an utterance of the LORD". It marks the next words as the LORD's own.
b: Ne'um is a noun, "utterance", from a root meaning to murmur or speak; the phrase ne'um YHWH is in the prophets over three hundred times and in the Plain is "the LORD declares". It appears in Joel only here, and in 2:12 it breaks into the prophet's own speech with words marked as the LORD's. The chapter's turning point is in these two words and the one that precedes them, gam 'attah, "Even now".

p: The Hebrew verb is shuv, "turn", the prophets' word for repentance.
b: Shuv means to turn around and go back. The prophets use it for returning to the LORD (Hosea 14:1-2; Jeremiah 3:12-14; 4:1; Zechariah 1:3; Malachi 3:7). In Joel the same verb will also describe what the LORD does in return: "He may turn back and change his mind" (2:14). The verb thus joins the people's turning and the LORD's. The Plain always writes "turn back" for this verb in a prophet's call, as in Jeremiah, so the reader can see it.

a: Tear your hearts and not your clothes
p: Tearing one's clothes was the normal sign of grief. Joel asks for an inward tearing, and the line became famous.
b: To tear one's clothes was the ordinary public sign of grief or alarm (Genesis 37:34; Joshua 7:6; 2 Kings 19:1). Joel does not forbid it; he asks that the heart be torn first. The same spirit is in Psalm 51:17 (a broken and crushed heart), Jeremiah 4:4 (circumcise your hearts), Isaiah 58:5-7 and Hosea 6:6. In the Mishnah (Taanit 2:1), on a fast day for rain, the elder among them addresses the people with words of warning and quotes this verse, together with Jonah 3:10, to say that God looks at what people do, not only at sackcloth and fasting.

p: Joel quotes the description of himself that the LORD gave Moses at Sinai, and changes its ending.
b: In Exodus 34:6-7 the LORD passes before Moses and says: "a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness, keeping loyal love to thousands, forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin. Yet he will by no means leave guilt unpunished." The phrase "gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and great in loyal love" is repeated in Nehemiah 9:17 (the Plain's wording), Psalm 145:8 and Jonah 4:2; Psalm 86:15 and Psalm 103:8 turn the first two words around, as Exodus does. Joel's version has three differences: it puts "gracious" before "compassionate" (as Nehemiah and Psalm 145 do, unlike Exodus); it leaves out "faithfulness", "forgiving guilt" and the warning that the guilty are not cleared; and it ends with "he changes his mind about the harm", a line that Exodus does not have but Jonah 4:2 shares. The creed is thus turned to the use of Joel's moment: not what God does with sin in general, but what he may do with this disaster.
r: Exodus 34:6; Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8; Jonah 4:2

a: he changes his mind about the harm
p: The Hebrew verb nicham is used of God again and again. The Plain uses "change his mind", as in Jeremiah.
b: The Hebrew nicham can mean "be sorry", "relent" or "change one's mind", and the Bible uses it of God to say that he does not carry out a threatened harm when people turn back (Jeremiah 18:7-10; 26:3, 13; Exodus 32:14; Amos 7:3, 6; Jonah 3:10). The Plain follows its Jeremiah and uses "change his mind about the harm"; the older English "repent" suggests that God had sinned. Other texts say that God "does not change his mind" as a man does (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29), and churches read the two sets together in different ways (see the card on 2:12-14). The word for "harm" is ra'ah, the same word as "evil" when people do it; the Plain says "harm" when God is the one who plans it.
r: Exodus 32:14; Jeremiah 18:8; Jeremiah 26:3; Amos 7:3; Jonah 3:10; Numbers 23:19

a: slow to anger and great in loyal love
t: What the scrolls have of the creed
p: The scroll 4Q78 preserves most of the creed and agrees with the Masoretic Text; 4Q82 stops early.
b: The scroll 4Q78 (4QXII-c) preserves this verse: the words "gracious and compassionate", "great in loyal love" and "changes his mind" are visible and match the Masoretic Text, "slow to anger" and "the harm" are restored, and "your hearts" has a longer spelling. The scroll 4Q82 (4QXII-g) breaks off after "turn back to the LORD your God".

p: "Who knows?" is the repenter's honest word: God owes nothing, but he may relent.
b: The same phrase is in David's words about his sick child (2 Samuel 12:22: "Who knows? The LORD might show me favor, and the boy would live") and in the Ninevite king's hope in Jonah 3:9; compare Amos 5:15 and Zephaniah 2:3. It is not doubt that God is kind, which Joel has just affirmed, but the recognition that repenting is a plea and not a purchase. A plea can still be met, as the next verses show. The same "who knows" in the Ninevite king's mouth is answered with a plain statement of what God did (Jonah 3:10).

t: A blessing that lets worship resume
p: The blessing is the harvest, which will make offerings possible again.
b: "Leave behind him a blessing" is the opposite of the army that left a desert behind it (2:3). The blessing is spelled out at once: grain and drink offerings, the very things cut off in 1:9 and 1:13. Joel therefore wants the harvest back for a reason as well as a hunger: so that the worship of the LORD can go on. The LORD's relenting and the nation's worship are bound together.

p: Joel 2:12-18 is the first reading at Mass on Ash Wednesday, and Joel 2:1-2, 12-17 is the common lectionary's reading for the day.
b: The Roman Catholic lectionary reads Joel 2:12-18 at Mass on Ash Wednesday, the first day of Lent, and the Revised Common Lectionary (used by many Protestant churches) gives Joel 2:1-2, 12-17 or Isaiah 58:1-12. The call "Turn back to me with your whole heart" (2:12) opens the season of penitence, and the ashes laid on the forehead are a Christian form of the sackcloth and ashes of the prophets. The Orthodox begin Great Lent on Clean Monday with a similar call to repentance but do not mark the day with ashes. The practice is a later church use of Joel; Joel himself does not mention ashes. See the card on fasting.

p: Even babies and newlyweds are called. In this crisis no one is excused.
b: A newly married man was normally excused from military service and public duty for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5). Joel calls the bridegroom and the bride out and brings the nursing babies to the gathering. This is the language of a national emergency: everyone, the old, the small and the newly married, stands before the LORD (compare 2 Chronicles 20:13, where Judah stands with its little ones; Jonah 3:7-8, where even animals fast). The call to the bride and groom has a second effect: wedding joy gives way to repentance, just as the "young woman" is told to mourn in 1:8.

a: Between the porch and the altar
p: The porch and the altar were the open space in front of the Temple building, the place where the priests could be seen by all.
b: The "porch" ('ulam) was the entrance hall of the Temple and the altar of burnt offering stood in the court in front of it (1 Kings 6:3; 8:64; Ezekiel 8:16). Priests who stand between them are in the open, facing the people, with their backs to the sanctuary. In Matthew 23:35 Jesus uses "between the sanctuary and the altar" for the place of the killing of Zechariah (see Matthew 23:35; 2 Chronicles 24:20-21). Solomon too prayed at the altar before all the assembly (1 Kings 8:22).

a: to nations who would rule over them
p: The Hebrew can mean "rule over them" or "make them a byword". The Greek and Latin took "rule".
b: The Masoretic pointing reads limshol, the infinitive of mashal "rule", giving "so that nations rule over them" (the Greek and the KJV). The same consonants can be pointed lemashal, "for a byword" (the noun mashal, "proverb, byword", as in Psalm 44:14), giving "a byword among the nations" (the choice of many modern versions, matching the parallel word "disgrace"). They are two words of the same spelling. Both fit: to be ruled is to be mocked. The Plain takes "rule" because that is the reading of the oldest translations and of the Hebrew pointing, and notes the other. The scroll 4Q78 (4QXII-c) preserves these consonants without vowels, so it cannot tell the two apart. The people's Temple and land are the LORD's "inheritance", so disgrace to them is disgrace to him.

p: The priests quote the nations' taunt, which is also in the psalms, as part of their plea.
b: The same question is in Psalm 79:10, Psalm 115:2 and Micah 7:10. It is an argument: if the people fall, the nations will say that their God is weak. Moses uses the same argument for Israel in Exodus 32:12 and Numbers 14:13-16, and Joel's priests rest the plea on it, because the LORD's "name" is on his people (2:26-27). The people's suffering damages God's reputation, so rescuing them is also rescuing his name. The mocking of God is the heart of the prayer, not the people's own pain.

a: Then the LORD burned with jealousy for his land
t: The turning point, and a question of tense
p: The Hebrew can be read as a past event, the LORD answering, or as the start of a promise.
b: The two verbs of 2:18 are in the Hebrew form that usually tells what happened next, so most read: after the assembly, the LORD acted, and the following verses are his answer. Others point out that there is no report of the assembly, and that the verses after it are in the future; so they read 2:18 as a promise: "Then the LORD will be jealous...". The Greek and the Latin read it as past. If it is past, Joel records the answer to the people's prayer; if future, the book is a promise to the community that repents. The book would still end the same way. "Jealous" (qana') is the word for the LORD's fierce commitment to his own, in the Ten Words and elsewhere (Exodus 20:5; Zechariah 1:14; 8:2).

a: the new wine and the fresh oil
p: These three together are the standard list of the land's gifts, which the covenant promised and its curses took away.
b: The triple of grain, new wine and fresh oil (dagan, tirosh, yitshar) is the standard way of saying the harvest in Deuteronomy 7:13; 11:14; 12:17; 28:51 and in Hosea 2:8-9, 22. The blessings and curses of the covenant promise these when Israel obeys and take them away when Israel does not (Deuteronomy 28:38-42, 51). Joel returns to the list at 1:10 (all three failed) and 2:24 (all three restored), so that the book's course is a trip around the list.

t: Who or what is the northern one?
p: The Hebrew has "the northerner", a rare form, and ancient and modern readers differ on whom it means.
b: The locusts. The locust plague is the enemy driven out; but locust swarms in Israel normally come from the south or east (Exodus 10:13), not the north. A human army. The north is where Israel's invaders came from, Assyria and Babylon (Jeremiah 1:14-15; Zephaniah 2:13). An end-time foe. In Ezekiel 38-39 Gog comes "from the far north" (Ezekiel 38:15); later interpreters have therefore taken this as the enemy of the last days. A symbol. The north was the home of the gods in Canaanite thought (Isaiah 14:13), and "the northern one" is the chaos-power. The word is a singular with the article, which fits a swarm or a power better than a named people. The Plain says "the northern one", no more.

a: its front into the eastern sea
p: The eastern sea is the Dead Sea; the western sea is the Mediterranean.
b: The "eastern sea" is the Dead Sea (compare Ezekiel 47:18; Zechariah 14:8) and the "western sea" the Mediterranean (the "Great Sea" of Numbers 34:6). The vanguard goes into one and the rear guard into the other, so that the whole line is wiped out, from front to back. It is also true that a swarm blown out to sea by a strong wind ends up in the sea and washes up in heaps on the shore; the stench that rises, then, is natural, and Exodus 10:19 (a west wind carried the Egyptian locusts into the Sea of Reeds) offers a parallel.

a: for he has done great things
p: "He" may be the LORD, or the northern one boasting of his deeds. The same phrase is used of the LORD in the next verse.
b: The Hebrew higdil la'asot is "he has made great to do", and the same words in 2:21 have "the LORD" as the subject. In 2:20 the subject is left out: the LORD may be said to have done great things (as in Psalm 126:2-3), or the northern one may have acted proudly (as Moab in Jeremiah 48:26: "he has made himself great against the LORD"). The Greek takes the second sense, "for he has magnified his works". The Plain's "he" keeps the doubt. The scroll Mur88 preserves the words "for he has done great things" without a subject, as the Masoretic Text has them (in 4Q78 they are restored). See the variant.

a: I will thrust it into a dry and empty land
t: What did the Jewish commentators make of the northern one?
p: Rashi gives three readings, locusts, Assyria and the evil inclination; Ibn Ezra and Radak take the locust.
b: Rashi gives three readings: a locust swarm (which suits the "dry and empty land"), the kings of Assyria, and the evil inclination, following the Sages in Sukkah 52a, who read hatsefoni as tsafun, "hidden", the one hidden in a person's heart. Ibn Ezra takes it as the locust army that came from the north. Radak also takes the locust, called northern because it came from that side, and records the rabbinic reading of the evil inclination. The scroll 4Q78 (4QXII-c) preserves "the northern one" and "I will drive far from you" in its visible words, and Mur88 preserves "I will drive far from you" with "the northern one" restored.

t: The reversal begins with the land
p: The land, then the animals, then the people are told to stop fearing and start rejoicing. The order matches the order of the loss.
b: The land mourned first (1:10), then the animals groaned (1:18, 20), then the people were told to rejoice no more (1:12, 16). The promise runs the same way: the land is told to be glad (2:21), the animals not to fear (2:22), the people to rejoice (2:23). The command "do not be afraid" is the common beginning of a salvation oracle, the LORD's message of rescue to someone in danger (Isaiah 41:10, 14; 43:1, 5; Lamentations 3:57). Here it is spoken to the ground itself. The word for "land" is 'adamah, the soil, the same as the mourning "ground" of 1:10.

a: the early rain to set things right
p: Hammoreh can mean "early rain" or "teacher"; the Latin has "teacher of righteousness", the Greek "food".
b: Moreh means "rain" (the "early rain", Psalm 84:6; Deuteronomy 11:14) or "teacher" (from yarah, to teach), and litsedaqah can mean "for righteousness", "in due measure" or "for vindication". So the line is "he has given you the early rain to set things right" (most modern versions, fitted to the second half of the verse where moreh is plainly "rain") or "he has given you the teacher for righteousness". The Vulgate has doctorem iustitiae, and Christian writers such as Jerome applied it to Christ. The Greek (Rahlfs and Swete both number it 2:23) has "the food for righteousness". The Plain says "the early rain to set things right": the LORD has put things right. "Children of Zion" is benei Tsiyyon, as in Psalm 149:2 ("Zion's children") and Lamentations 4:2 ("The sons of Zion").

a: the early rain and the spring rain, as before
p: Israel's rain falls in two seasons, autumn and spring. Joel promises both.
b: The "early rain" (yoreh or moreh) comes in October and November and softens the ground for plowing; the "spring rain" (malqosh) falls in March and April and fills out the grain (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24; Hosea 6:3; Zechariah 10:1; James 5:7). A failure of either meant famine. The last Hebrew word, barishon, "at first", can mean "as before" (most versions) or "in the first month" (the KJV), that is, at the start of the year. The Plain takes "as before", which fits the promise of 2:25 to restore what was lost.

a: He has sent down rain for you
p: Rashi also reads "teacher", meaning the prophets. The Qumran Teacher of Righteousness is a separate matter.
b: Rashi also takes the first moreh as "teacher", meaning the prophets who teach Israel to turn back, and the second as rain (Deuteronomy 11:14). The title "the Teacher of Righteousness" (moreh hatsedeq) belongs to the founder of the Qumran community in the Damascus Document and the Habakkuk commentary; but those texts do not quote Joel 2:23, and the scroll 4Q78 (4QXII-c) preserves these words with the same consonants as the Masoretic Text. Linking the two is a modern guess.

a: I will give you back the years
p: The promise is a sign of the LORD's care. Some modern teaching turns it into a formula for personal wealth.
b: The Hebrew shillamti means "I will repay, make up for" and the promise is that the harvests lost to the locusts will be made up by years of plenty. It is a promise to the nation, in a time of crop failure, from the LORD who sent the plague. Some modern preachers use "I will restore the years the locust has eaten" as a promise that God will repay every lost year or opportunity in a believer's life. That is a modern use that moves the promise from the nation's fields to an individual, and the Plain's reader should keep the setting in mind. Others, in a weaker sense, apply it as a picture of God's repair of damage.
orig: וְשִׁלַּמְתִּי לָכֶם אֶת הַשָּׁנִים (veshillamti lakhem et hashanim)

a: my great army that I sent among you
p: The plague is the LORD's doing, as in the covenant curses.
b: The covenant said that locusts would eat the crops of an unfaithful nation (Deuteronomy 28:38, 42; 1 Kings 8:37), and Amos names locusts among the plagues the LORD sent that did not bring the people back to him (Amos 4:9; Amos 7:1). Psalm 78:46 and 105:34-35 count the locusts of Egypt among the LORD's acts. Joel's "my army" is a plain claim: the LORD commanded the plague, so the LORD can end it.

a: the hopping locust, the stripping locust
t: Claude's theory: the order of the four locusts is turned around
p: In 1:4 the order is cutting, swarming, hopping, stripping. Here it is swarming, hopping, stripping, cutting.
b: My own observation, not a standard view. The four names return in a different order: the first of 1:4 (gazam, "cutting") moves to the end, so the series begins with the best known of them, the swarm ('arbeh), the name used for the Egyptian plague, and ends with gazam. The Greek Bible shows the same shift, which makes it likely that the Hebrew order was already fixed. Commentators note the change and some explain it as variety for its own sake. A possible explanation: 1:4 names the four as the plague actually came, and 2:25 names them as a list of what the LORD will repay, in the order of the last to the first, or in the order of the Exodus text (Exodus 10:4, 12-15 has 'arbeh only). I have not found a published argument for either; read it as a suggestion.

p: The claim that the LORD alone is God is made at the end of the plague's story, as it was at the end of Egypt's.
b: Deuteronomy 4:35, 39 and Isaiah 45:5-6, 18, 21-22 say that the LORD is God and there is no other. In Exodus the plague of locusts was sent so that Israel would "know that I am the LORD" (Exodus 10:2). Joel 2:27 repeats the idea of recognition: "You will know that I am among Israel, that I am the LORD your God". The line closes the first half of the book and the pair of promises of 2:26 and 2:27: your shame is ended because your God is in your midst.

a: My people will never be ashamed.
t: Claude's theory: shame opens and closes the plague story
p: The book's first command to farmers is "Be ashamed" (1:11). Its last promise before the Spirit is "never ashamed".
b: My own observation, built on the wordplay in 1:10-12. In the Hebrew the same root bosh, "be ashamed", is used for the farmers (1:11) and for the promise twice repeated in 2:26 and 2:27. The first time the people are put to shame by a failed harvest; the last time they are promised that this shame will not return. If the line is repeated on purpose, it marks the end of the first half of the book, as an echo of its start. Commentators note the repeated sentence (Wolff, Crenshaw); I know of no one who ties it to the opening command, so treat the link as a suggestion.

a: After this, I will pour out my Spirit
p: In Hebrew this is chapter 3. Greek editions differ: Rahlfs numbers like the Hebrew, Swete like the English.
b: The Hebrew Bible numbers these five verses as Joel 3:1-5, so Hebrew Joel has four chapters (20, 27, 5 and 21 verses), and English chapter 3 is Hebrew chapter 4. The Greek editions differ. Rahlfs's Septuagint and the Greek Orthodox lectionary number as the Hebrew does (the lectionary reads "Joel 2:23-3:5" for English 2:23-32); the printout of Swete's edition used for this site, the Vulgate and the English Bibles number 2:28-32 and 3:1-21. This Plain, its notes and its references use the English numbers; where a note gives the Greek it says "Rahlfs" or "Swete". "After this" is acharei khen, "afterward"; the Greek has meta tauta and Peter in Acts 2:17 changes it to "in the last days". The Greek also has "from my Spirit" (see the variant).
orig: אַחֲרֵי כֵן אֶשְׁפּוֹךְ אֶת רוּחִי (acharei khen 'eshpokh 'et ruchi)

p: "Flesh" means human beings and, here, probably the people of Israel. Whether it means everyone is the question.
b: Basar, "flesh", is a Hebrew way of saying "human beings" in their weakness (Psalm 56:4; Isaiah 40:6). "All flesh" is used for the whole human race in Genesis 6:12-13 and Isaiah 66:23, but the next words in Joel ("your sons and daughters", "your old men", "the male slaves") speak to Israel. So "all flesh" is either everyone in the nation, of every age, sex and rank, or Israel at first and every nation afterward. Peter takes the second sense in Acts 2:39. In Numbers 11:29 Moses wished that all the LORD's people were prophets; Joel gives the wish an answer. The Plain keeps "flesh" so that the reader can see the word.

a: They will prophesy, your sons and your daughters
p: Peter quotes Joel 2:28-32 at Pentecost. His wording follows the Greek Bible, with some changes of his own.
b: Acts 2:17-21 quotes these verses. Peter follows the Greek of Joel (the Septuagint) with these differences: he begins "in the last days" for "after this" and adds "God says"; he puts the young men's visions before the old men's dreams; he puts "my" before both "slaves" and "slave women" (the Greek of Joel in Swete's printout has it only before the men) and adds "and they will prophesy"; he adds "up in the sky" and "down on the earth" and "signs" to "wonders"; and he says "that great and shining day" for the Hebrew's "great and awesome day" (the Greek of Joel also has "shining", epiphane). Peter's claim in Acts 2:16 is that "this is the very thing spoken through Joel the prophet". Peter and the Greek of Joel agree with each other, against the Hebrew, in "pour out from my Spirit" (see the note on verse numbers above and the variant); the Plain of Acts 2:17-18 has "I will pour out my Spirit" and does not show it. Elsewhere the New Testament uses the language of pouring out the Spirit without quoting Joel: Acts 2:33, Acts 10:45 (on the Gentiles in Cornelius's house) and Titus 3:5-6. How "this is that" works is debated: it may mean fulfillment, a partial fulfillment, or the same kind of event. See the card.
r: Acts 2:16; Acts 2:17; Acts 2:18; Acts 2:21; Acts 2:39; Acts 2:33; Acts 10:45; Titus 3:5

a: Your old men will have dreams
p: Dreams and visions were two accepted ways in which the LORD spoke to prophets.
b: The LORD says in Numbers 12:6 that he makes himself known to a prophet "in a vision" and speaks "in a dream". Joel says that all ages will now have what was once a prophet's gift: the old dream, the young see visions. In the normal order of Israelite society, the old were the teachers and the young the learners; here the gift is not tied to age. Acts 2:17 reverses the order (the young men see visions and the older men have dreams); the reason for the change is not known.

a: the male slaves and the female slaves
p: The Hebrew eved is "servant" or "slave". Here the point is that the lowest rank receives the Spirit too.
b: 'Eved and shifchah are the male and female slaves of a household. The Plain says "slaves" because the contrast is social: sons and daughters, old and young, then the slaves. The gift of the Spirit goes to the bottom of society as well as the top. In the Hebrew Bible the Spirit rested on a few leaders, judges, kings and prophets; here it is given to those who had no voice in the assembly. The Greek of Joel (Swete's printout) has "my" before the male slaves, and Acts 2:18 has it before both, so that Peter's slaves are the LORD's slaves; Galatians 3:28 draws a similar line between slave and free.

a: I will pour out my Spirit in those days
p: Ruach is "Spirit", "wind" and "breath". The Plain uses a capital where the LORD's own Spirit is meant.
b: "Spirit" is ruach, the same word as "wind" and "breath"; where the LORD's own Spirit is meant the Plain writes it with a capital. "Pour out" is shafakh, used of water (Isaiah 44:3) and of blood; it is the word of Ezekiel 39:29, where the LORD says he has poured out his Spirit on the house of Israel.

a: I will set wonders in the heavens and on the earth
p: The Hebrew mofet is a wonder or portent. "Pillars of smoke" is the same word used for the smoke of the desert march.
b: Mofet is used for the signs of the Exodus, the "wonders" of Egypt (Exodus 7:3; 11:9-10; Deuteronomy 4:34). "Pillars of smoke" (timrot 'ashan) appears also in Song of Songs 3:6, where the bride comes up from the wilderness "like pillars of smoke". The three signs, blood, fire and smoke, may be the signs of war (Isaiah 9:18) or of a volcanic or fiery sky, or of the smoke of burnt cities. Acts 2:19 has "a haze of smoke" from the Greek. The Plain keeps the Hebrew order: the wonders are set, then the three signs are named.

p: This is the one place in the Old Testament where the moon turns to blood. The New Testament picks it up.
b: Isaiah 13:10, Ezekiel 32:7-8 and Joel 2:10 speak of the sun and moon growing dark; only Joel 2:31 says "the moon into blood". The colors may describe a total eclipse of the sun and a reddish lunar eclipse, or the red haze of a dust storm, or poetic language for the end of an age. Acts 2:20 quotes the verse. Revelation 6:12 takes it up in the sixth seal: "The sun became black like sackcloth made of hair, and all of the moon became like blood." The Plain of Joel and the Plain of Revelation agree wherever the Hebrew and Greek words are the same. See the topic page on signs in the sky.

a: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be rescued
t: "Calls on the name of the LORD"
p: Peter and Paul quote this verse. In Hebrew it speaks of escaping; in Greek of being saved.
b: The Greek of Joel is numbered 2:32 in Swete's printout and 3:5 in Rahlfs. To "call on the name of the LORD" is to pray to him and worship him by name (Genesis 4:26; Psalm 116:4, 13, 17; Zephaniah 3:9). The Hebrew yimmalet means "escape" or "be delivered" (it is the verb of the "escaped" survivors later in the verse), and the Greek sothesetai is the ordinary word for "be saved". In Acts 2:21 Peter ends his quotation of Joel here; Paul quotes the verse in Romans 10:13: "For anyone at all who calls on the Lord's name will be saved." In Greek the word for "LORD" (kyrios) stands for the divine name, and Paul in Romans 10:9-13 applies it to Jesus as Lord. That shows how early Christians read a verse about the LORD's name as a verse about Jesus. The Plain keeps the two languages apart: it writes "rescued" for the Hebrew yimmalet here and "saved" for the Greek sothesetai in Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13, so a reader who follows the quotation sees two English words for one thought. Jewish readers keep the Hebrew sense: those who call on God by his name in Jerusalem will be delivered.
orig: יִקְרָא בְּשֵׁם יְהוָה יִמָּלֵט (yiqra' beshem YHWH yimmalet)

t: Survivors and those who are left
p: Two words for survivors, peletah and sarid, describe those who live through the day.
b: Peletah is "escape" or "survivors", from the verb malat in the first half of the verse; sarid is "one who is left", a remnant (Judges 5:13; Isaiah 1:9). The verse says that the LORD himself "calls" the survivors. "Those whom the LORD calls" may be the same group as "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD": the human call and the LORD's call meet. The remnant on Mount Zion is the promise of rescue within the judgment, the theme that Obadiah 17 echoes ("on Mount Zion there will be survivors"). At the end of the verse the Greek has kai euangelizomenoi, "and those who bring good news", where the Hebrew has uvassridim, "and among the survivors"; the translator probably read the consonants as a form of basar, "bring news" (Greek 3:5 in Rahlfs). Paul quotes the first half of the verse in Romans 10:13 and speaks of those who bring good news in 10:15, but he does not quote that clause of Joel. See the variant.

a: For look, in those days and at that time,
p: The Hebrew Bible starts a new chapter here. The Hebrew verses 4:1-21 are English 3:1-21.
b: In the Hebrew Bible this verse is Joel 4:1, because Hebrew chapter 3 is only the five verses that the English count as 2:28-32. The Vulgate, Swete's printout of the Greek and the English Bibles number the verses 3:1-21; Rahlfs's Greek and the Greek Orthodox lectionary number them as the Hebrew does, 4:1-21. A "for" opens the chapter, tying it to the promise of 2:32: the survivors on Zion are the ones who will see these things. Verses 1-3 set the date of the judgment, "in those days and at that time", language that has no fixed calendar date (compare Jeremiah 33:15; Zephaniah 3:20). The chapter is one continuous unit with 2:28-32 for most commentators; some see a different hand in chapters 3 and 4 of the Hebrew.

a: turn the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem around
t: Fortunes or captives? And a Ketiv
p: The phrase shuv shevut can mean "restore the fortunes" or "bring back the captives".
b: The idiom shuv shevut (also spelled shevit) is used for a reversal of fortune in Job 42:10 as well as for the return of exiles in Jeremiah 29:14; 30:3; 33:7 (the Plain: "turn the fortunes around"). The word may come from shavah, "take captive", or from shuv, "turn", and its sense is debated; the phrase is used for peoples (Sodom and Samaria) that were not exiled, so "restore the fortunes" is the most likely sense. Joel's use, with "Judah and Jerusalem", is read as a sign of a time after the exile by those who date the book late; those who date it early read it as a reversal of fortune that follows the plague, since no exile is named in this verse. The Hebrew text has a Ketiv/Qere here: the written text (Ketiv) has 'ashuv, "I will turn", and the reading tradition (Qere) has 'ashiv, "I will cause to turn". The sense is the same. The scroll Mur88 has "those days" with a different spelling (hahi for hahem) and its verb is restored, so it cannot decide. See the variant.

t: Where is the Valley of Jehoshaphat?
p: The name means "the LORD judges". Is it a real valley near Jerusalem, a place in a story, or a name for the last judgment?
b: Yehoshafat means "the LORD judges" and the verse (and 3:12) plays on it: this is where he judges. A symbolic name: most modern commentators take the name as a name made for the occasion, as Isaiah 7:3 names Shear-jashub, because no valley by this name is known in the Bible. A real valley: the valley of Beracah, where King Jehoshaphat's army won without fighting (2 Chronicles 20:20-26), near Tekoa has been suggested. The Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem: from the fourth century on the valley between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives was called by that name (the Bordeaux Pilgrim, AD 333, names a valley called "Josaphat" on the road from the eastern gate up to the Mount of Olives), and Jews, Christians and Muslims have buried their dead on its slopes in the hope of being near the judgment. The end-time battle: Christians have joined the valley to Zechariah 14:2-4, Ezekiel 38-39 and Revelation 16:16. The Jewish commentators. Rashi reads the name as "the LORD's judgments", a valley where God judges. Ibn Ezra says it is the Valley of Blessing (Beracah), which Jehoshaphat named (2 Chronicles 20:26). Radak says it is named either for King Jehoshaphat or for the judgment God will hold there. The Plain keeps the Hebrew name. See the topic page.
r: 2 Chronicles 20:26; Isaiah 7:3; Zechariah 14:2; Ezekiel 39:11; Revelation 16:16; Joel 3:12

a: whom they scattered among the nations
p: The charge is the scattering of Judah and the dividing of the land. What event is meant is the dating question.
b: The sins listed are: scattering the people among the nations, dividing up the land, casting lots for the people, and selling boys and girls (3:2-3, 6). If the speaker has the Babylonian conquest of 586 BC in view, "scattered" is the exile (2 Kings 25; Lamentations 1:3); the "dividing" of the land recalls the Edomite and others' land-grab described in Ezekiel 35:10 and 36:5. If an earlier raid is meant, 2 Chronicles 21:16-17 tells how the Philistines and Arabs carried off the goods and family of King Jehoram. In either case, the nations are judged for what they did to the LORD's "people and inheritance", and the language is the language of covenant: hurting Israel is hurting the LORD (Genesis 12:3; Zechariah 2:8).

a: They cast lots for my people
p: The nations treated the LORD's people as property to be shared out by lot. Other prophets use the same words.
b: "Cast lots for" captives is in Obadiah 11 and Nahum 3:10, both about the fall of cities. Selling a boy for a prostitute and a girl for wine is the language of a drunken market: the price of a human being is a night or a drink. The slave trade of the ancient world included war captives, and Amos 1:6, 9 accuses Gaza and Tyre of handing whole communities over to Edom. The point of the line is the cheapness of what was bought and sold. In the Masoretic Text the preposition is 'el; the scroll Mur88 and the Greek have 'al, which is the preposition Obadiah 11 and Nahum 3:10 use. See the variant.

p: The accused are the coastal cities that bought and sold people. Their crime is the slave trade.
b: Tyre and Sidon were the great Phoenician sea-traders; Philistia was the coastal plain of the five cities. Ezekiel 27:13 names the Greeks (Javan), Tubal and Meshech among those who traded with Tyre in the lives of men, and Amos 1:6-10 accuses Gaza and Tyre of handing over whole communities. 2 Chronicles 21:16-17 says the LORD stirred up the Philistines and Arabs against Jehoram of Judah and they carried off his sons and wives. The Hebrew word gelilot is "districts" or "circuits" (the Hebrew word that gave Galilee its name; the Greek translators read "Galilee of the foreigners", Rahlfs 4:4 and Swete 3:4). The scroll Mur88 reads "the districts of Philistia" as the Masoretic Text does; 4Q82 (4QXII-g) has a variant spelling of the first word. "What are you to me?" means: what claim do you have on me?

p: The Hebrew hekhal can mean a temple or a palace. The treasure taken was brought to the cities' great buildings.
b: Hekhal is the word for the Temple's main hall in Jerusalem and, more widely, for any grand building of a god or king (Psalm 45:8; Isaiah 39:7). The Greek has "temples". The charge is that the silver, gold and fine things of Judah, probably the treasure of the Temple and the king's house (compare 2 Chronicles 21:16-17), ended up as decoration in the buildings of Tyre, Sidon and Philistia. The verse does not say which event is meant.

p: The Hebrew has bene hayyevanim, "the sons of the Ionians". This is a rare mention of Greeks in the prophets.
b: Yavan is Ionia and, by extension, the Greeks. Genesis 10:2, 4 makes Javan a son of Japheth; Isaiah 66:19 names Javan among distant nations; Ezekiel 27:13, 19 lists Javan among the traders of Tyre who deal in slaves and bronze; Daniel 8:21 and 10:20 use it for the Greek kingdom (the Plain: "Greece"). Greek traders were active on the Syrian and Palestinian coast from about the eighth century BC. For those who date Joel late, Greek slave markets fit the Persian period or the time just before Alexander; for those who date him early, Greek traders in the ninth century are possible but not certain, and the early date has to find a place for them. The Plain writes "the Greeks". The scrolls 4Q82 (4QXII-g) and Mur88 both preserve "the sons of the Ionians" as the Masoretic Text has it.

p: Sheba was in southwest Arabia. The far-off buyers are the Sabeans.
b: Sheba (Sheva'), the land of the Sabeans in southern Arabia, was a distant source of incense, gold and spices (1 Kings 10:1-2; Isaiah 60:6; Jeremiah 6:20; Ezekiel 27:22) and the home of raiders in Job 1:15. To sell slaves to Sheba is to send them as far as the known world went. The law of equal return is at work: the Phoenicians and Philistines who sold Judeans to the Greeks will have their own sons and daughters sold, by Judeans, to a people even farther away (Obadiah 15). The Plain says "the people of Sheba", as in Job.

p: To "consecrate" war is to declare it a holy act. Joel gives the order to the nations.
b: The same verb is used for "consecrate a fast" (1:14; 2:15) and for the "consecrate war" of Jeremiah 6:4 (the Plain: "Consecrate war against her!"), Jeremiah 51:27 and Micah 3:5. In ancient Israel a war was begun with rites and sacrifice (1 Samuel 7:9; 13:9-12). Joel turns the summons upside down: it is the nations who are to prepare for a holy war, and the war they come to is the LORD's judgment (3:12). The word "warriors" in 3:9 and 3:11 is gibborim, the same word for the LORD's "warriors" in 3:11.

p: Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 have swords turned into plowshares. Joel reverses them for the war before the peace.
b: Isaiah 2:4 says of the nations in the last days: "They will pound their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning knives." Micah 4:3 has the same. Joel 3:10 reverses it: "Pound your plowshares into swords and your pruning knives into spears." Which saying is older is disputed: some think Joel answers Isaiah and Micah, some think Isaiah and Micah reverse Joel, and some think the saying is old and each prophet uses it for a purpose. Joel's order makes a sequence that others have also read: first the battle, then the peace. The tools of peace become tools of war because the summons in 3:9 is a call to arms. Compare the peace that follows in 3:16-21.

t: A prayer in the middle of the summons
p: The line breaks the summons with a prayer. The Hebrew verb is unusual and the Greek reads something different.
b: The Hebrew has hanchat, an unusual form of the verb "come down", and the Hebrew letters can be divided in other ways. The Greek (Rahlfs 4:11; Swete 3:11) reads "let the gentle (or humble) man be a fighter", the Vulgate reads "there the LORD will make your strong ones fall". The Plain keeps the Hebrew: the prophet turns to the LORD in the middle of the nations' call and asks him to send his own warriors, the angels or the hosts of heaven, as at Psalm 103:20 and Joel 2:11. See the variant.

a: for there I will sit to judge
t: The LORD seated as judge of the nations
p: The LORD sits in judgment on all the nations. Later writers use the same picture.
b: God sits as judge of the nations in Psalm 9:7-8 and Psalm 96:13, and Isaiah 66:18 speaks of the time when he will gather all nations and languages. Zechariah 14:2 has the nations gathered against Jerusalem. In the New Testament the Son of Man sits on his throne and all the nations are gathered before him (Matthew 25:31-32), and Revelation 20:11-15 has the great white throne. Whether those scenes are fulfillments of Joel 3, or only use its picture, is read differently by the churches (see the card).
r: Psalm 9:7; Psalm 96:13; Isaiah 66:18; Zechariah 14:2; Matthew 25:31; Revelation 20:11

p: The sickle and the winepress are pictures of judgment. Jesus and John use the sickle image.
b: In Joel the harvest is ripe and the winepress full because "their evil is great", the picture of nations ripe for judgment. The Greek of Joel has "send out sickles" (exapostellete drepana) and Mark 4:29 uses a similar phrase of the grain harvest (the Plain: "he sends in the sickle"). Revelation 14:14-20 builds a scene from this verse and Isaiah 63:1-6: the one on the cloud with a sickle, the angel who gathers the vine, and the winepress outside the city. Whether the harvest is wheat (the righteous gathered; Matthew 13:39) or grapes (the wicked trodden; Revelation 14:19-20) depends on the passage.

p: The Hebrew verb redu can mean "come down" or "tread". The Plain keeps both.
b: Redu can come from yarad, "go down" (into the winepress), or, as some think, from a second radah, "tread". The image of treading the press as judgment is also in Isaiah 63:3 and Lamentations 1:15, but both use another verb (darakh, with puroh for the press in Isaiah): the image is shared, the verb is not. The Greek (Rahlfs 4:13; Swete 3:13) has "enter, tread", and the Latin "come and go down". The Plain's "Come down and tread" keeps both. The scroll 4Q78 (4QXII-c) preserves "come, redu" with the same consonants as the Masoretic Text; in 4Q82 and Mur88 the word is restored. Revelation 14:19-20 and 19:15 use the treading for the final judgment. It is both a picture of joy at harvest and one of judgment. See the variant.

a: Crowds upon crowds in the valley of decision!
p: The Hebrew charuts can mean "decision", "a verdict" or "a threshing sledge".
b: Charuts comes from a root meaning "to cut, decide" and appears as "a decision" in 1 Kings 20:40, as "a threshing sledge" in Isaiah 28:27 and 41:15 (the Plain's "sledge" and "threshing board") and as "gold" in other places. The valley of decision is the place where the verdict is given (3:2, 12: "the LORD judges"); the valley of threshing is the place where the nations are threshed like grain, a picture that fits the harvest of 3:13. The Greek has "the valley of the verdict" (dike; Rahlfs 4:14, Swete 3:14) and the Vulgate "the valley of cutting" (concisio). Both senses fit; the Plain's "valley of decision" is the more familiar English, and the note keeps the other.

p: Amos 1:2 has the same two lines, and the Plain gives the same English for them.
b: The line "The LORD roars from Zion and gives out his voice from Jerusalem" is word for word Amos 1:2 in the Hebrew (Amos 1:2 has "He said:" before the two lines), and the Plain gives the same English for the same Hebrew. Joel 3:16 and Amos 1:2 are the clearest links between the two books, and the Hebrew order of the Twelve, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, may be due to such links; the Greek order puts Joel after Micah. The usual view is that one writer knew the other's words, but which borrowed is disputed (the usual late-date view is that Joel quotes Amos; the early-date view is that Amos quotes Joel). In Joel, the roar ends a scene of judgment and begins one of refuge for the LORD's people; in Amos it opens a book of judgment on Israel.

t: A voice that shakes heaven and earth
p: A Ugaritic poem says the storm god Baal "gives his voice" and the earth shakes. Psalm 18, 46 and 68 use the same wording for the LORD.
b: A poem from Ugarit on the Syrian coast (about 1300 BC), in the Baal cycle, says that Baal "gives his holy voice" from the clouds, and the earth shakes (the text is KTU 1.4 vii, as Frank Moore Cross discussed in Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic). Psalm 29 uses the phrase "the voice of the LORD" (qol YHWH) seven times for the thunder, and Joel's "the LORD gives out his voice" (2:11; 3:16) uses a close expression, natan qol, which is also used of the LORD's thunder in Psalm 18:13, Psalm 46:6 and Psalm 68:33. It is a shared poetic language of the storm, and the Bible puts it in the mouth of the LORD, not Baal. It is not a borrowing of the Baal story, which Joel does not use; it shows that the picture of a God whose voice shakes heaven and earth was a common one, and the prophets claim it for the LORD.

a: outsiders will never pass through her again
p: The promise is that Jerusalem will be safe from invaders. Is it also a ban on foreigners?
b: The Hebrew zarim is "outsiders" (Isaiah 1:7; Lamentations 5:2) and "pass through" is the language of armies marching through a land (Isaiah 8:8; Nahum 1:15). Most commentators read the line as the end of invasion: the city will not be overrun again. Others read it as a ban on foreigners, against the hope of other prophets that the foreigner will come to the LORD's house (Isaiah 56:3-8; Zechariah 14:16). Both ideas are in the Bible, and the Plain leaves the word "outsiders". For the sense of Jerusalem as "holy", compare Isaiah 52:1 (the unclean will not enter again) and Revelation 21:27.

a: sweet wine will drip from the mountains
p: Amos 9:13 shares the first clause in Hebrew and differs in the second. It is the last promise of Joel; Amos has it near his end.
b: Amos 9:13, near the end of Amos, has "The mountains will drip with sweet wine" and "all the hills will flow with it" in the Plain, and Joel 3:18 has sweet wine dripping from the mountains and milk running down the hills. The first clauses share their Hebrew words in the same order, verb, mountains, sweet wine (Joel yitfu heharim 'asis, Amos vehittifu heharim 'asis), but the verb is not the same form (Joel's simple "drip", Amos's causative "make drip"); the English of Joel puts the wine first, so the match does not show. The second clauses differ: Joel's hills telakhnah chalav, "go with milk", Amos's hills titmogagnah, "melt" or "flow". The images are of the land of Canaan as the land flowing with milk and honey (Exodus 3:8), made even richer. The "sweet wine" is the same word ('asis) as in Joel 1:5, where it was cut off: the book ends where it began, with wine, but now it is the land that pours it.

a: A spring will flow out from the house of the LORD
p: A spring from the LORD's house waters the dry valley. Ezekiel, Zechariah and Revelation have the same picture.
b: Ezekiel 47:1-12 sees a stream flowing east from beneath the Temple's threshold, deepening as it goes, and bringing life to the Dead Sea. The Plain of Ezekiel 47:1 has water "flowing out from beneath the threshold, heading east". Zechariah 14:8 has living water flowing from Jerusalem east and west, and Revelation 22:1 has "a river of the water of life" from the throne of God. The pattern goes back to the river of Eden (Genesis 2:10) and to the river whose channels gladden the city of God (Psalm 46:4). Joel's spring is the shortest form of this picture: the Temple is the source of fertility, and its supply of water is the sign that God is there.

p: Shittim ("acacias") is a place on the east side of the Jordan. The spring will reach even the driest place.
b: Shittim is the plural of the acacia tree. A place of that name on the plains of Moab, opposite Jericho, is where Israel camped before crossing the Jordan (Numbers 25:1; Joshua 2:1; 3:1; Micah 6:5). "The wadi of Shittim" has been taken by some as a dry valley running down to the Dead Sea from there, and by others as a name for any acacia-covered wadi in the desert. Either way the spring from the Temple reaches the farthest and driest place, the same direction as the water in Ezekiel 47, which flows down to the Dead Sea. The Plain writes the place name as in Numbers 25:1.

p: Egypt and Edom stand for Judah's enemies. Both are to the south, and both did violence to Judah.
b: Egypt's king Shishak raided Judah in the days of Rehoboam and carried off the Temple treasures (1 Kings 14:25-26; 2 Chronicles 12:2-9), and Pharaoh Necho killed Josiah and took Jehoahaz away (2 Kings 23:29-34). Edom revolted from Judah in Jehoram's day (2 Kings 8:20-22) and, according to Obadiah 10-14, Psalm 137:7, Lamentations 4:21-22 and Ezekiel 35, took part in the sack of 586 BC. Those who date Joel early look to Shishak and Jehoram; those who date him late look to Edom's part in 586. Egypt and Edom may also be examples for all the nations: one great power and one old family enemy. Later Jewish readers used "Edom" for Rome and for later Christendom; that is a use of the name and not what Joel means. The scroll 4Q82 (4QXII-g) follows the Masoretic Text in this verse; 4Q78 (4QXII-c) appears to repeat "to a wilderness", with the second occurrence visible and the first restored.
r: 1 Kings 14:25; 2 Kings 8:20; 2 Kings 23:29; Obadiah 10; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21

p: The verb means "declare innocent". It can mean pardon or vindicate, and the verse is hard in Hebrew and in the old translations.
b: The Hebrew has niqqeti damam lo niqqeti, "I will hold innocent their blood, [which] I did not hold innocent". The verb niqqah usually means to leave unpunished (Exodus 34:7; Jeremiah 30:11), and the whole could mean (1) "I will pardon their bloodguilt, which I had not pardoned" (the guilty will be forgiven), (2) "I will vindicate their blood, which I had not vindicated", that is, I will avenge the innocent blood shed in Judah (as in 3:19), or (3) "I will not leave unpunished the blood of theirs that I had not yet punished". The Greek reads "I will seek out their blood and I will not acquit", which is the same sense as (2) and (3). The Plain keeps the Hebrew word and the doubt. The last clause, "the LORD lives in Zion", is clear. The Vulgate keeps the Hebrew repetition ("I will clear their blood, which I had not cleared"). The scroll 4Q78 (4QXII-c) preserves "their blood", the second "I cleared" and the last clause; the first verb is restored, so the scroll does not show whether the Hebrew doubled the verb. The Greek is numbered 4:21 in Rahlfs and 3:21 in Swete. See the variant.

t: A last line about where he lives
p: The book ends with the LORD's address. Ezekiel ends with a similar name for the city.
b: The book begins with "the LORD's word" coming to a prophet and ends with the LORD "dwelling" in Zion (3:17, 21). The last line of Ezekiel gives the name of the new city as "The LORD is there" (Ezekiel 48:35). Zion is the LORD's holy mountain in Joel from 2:1, and everything in the book, the alarm, the fast, the Spirit and the judgment of the nations, has been tied to that place.
